Medium · 

Semua tulisan

I am currently learning remote sensing and experimenting with different approaches for land cover analysis. In this exploration, I used Sentinel-2 imagery to distinguish mangroves based on their spectral characteristics.

hierarchy.lvl1: Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification
Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification

records.content:
First, I obtained Sentinel-2 imagery from the Copernicus Open Access Hub. The selected image covers the area of interest during a season with minimal cloud cover to ensure high-quality data.

Copernicus Browser

hierarchy.lvl1: Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification
Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification

records.content:
To enhance mangrove visibility, I applied an 8–11–4 composite (NIR-SWIR-Red).

Band 8 (NIR) highlights vegetation. Band 11 (SWIR) differentiates moisture content. Band 4 (Red) helps detect vegetation stress. In this composite, mangroves appear orange, but with varying brightness levels. This spectral difference provided a way to separate mangroves from other vegetation.

hierarchy.lvl1: Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification
Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification

records.content:
To further enhance the distinction of mangroves, I calculated two key indices using the following formulas:

NDMI (Normalized Difference Moisture Index):

The Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI) is an extension of NDVI, designed to assess the water content in vegetation. It was originally proposed by Gao (1996) and utilizes the Near-Infrared (NIR) and Shortwave Infrared (SWIR) bands

“NDWI index is often used synonymously with the NDMI index, often using NIR-SWIR combination as one of the two options. Gao, referenced above, also called the index NDWI. NDMI seems to be consistently described using NIR-SWIR combination. As the indices with these two combinations work very differently, with NIR-SWIR highlighting differences in water content of leaves, and GREEN-NIR highlighting differences in water content of water bodies, we have decided to separate the indices on our repository as NDMI using NIR-SWIR, and NDWI using GREEN-NIR” (

sentinelhub.com)NDMI = (B8 - B11) / (B8 + B11)

hierarchy.lvl1: Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification
Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification

records.content:
The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is a widely used remote sensing index that measures vegetation health and biomass. It was first introduced by Rouse et al. (1974) as a way to monitor plant growth and ecosystem dynamics using satellite imagery. NDVI is calculated using the reflectance values of the Near-Infrared (NIR) and Red bands:

Where: NIR (Near-Infrared, ~0.76–0.9 µm): Strongly reflected by healthy vegetation. Red (~0.63–0.69 µm): Strongly absorbed by chlorophyll in plants. NDVI values range from -1 to +1:NDVI = (B8 - B4) / (B8 + B4)

hierarchy.lvl1: Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification
Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification

records.content:
Using the Raster Calculator in ArcGIS, I classified mangrove areas using the following conditional formula:Con((NDMI > 0.2) & (NDVI > 0.3) & ((B8 / B11) > 1.2), 1, 0)

NDMI > 0.2 identifies moisture-rich vegetation. NDVI > 0.3 ensures that the area is covered with vegetation. NIR/SWIR Ratio (B8 / B11) > 1.2 distinguishes mangroves from other vegetation types.

hierarchy.lvl1: Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification
Exploring Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-2 and Threshold-Based Classification

records.content: After classification, I overlaid the results on the Sentinel-2 imagery to validate the extracted mangrove areas. The classified map effectively separated mangrove and non-mangrove regions.

NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine

records.content:
30 March 2025 · Terbit pertama di 

Medium · 

Semua tulisan

In remote sensing analysis, one of the key parameters used to monitor water presence is the Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI). NDWI is calculated using satellite imagery, one of which comes from Sentinel-2, provided by the European Union’s Copernicus program. In this article, we will use Google Earth Engine (GEE) to calculate NDWI from Sentinel-2 data and visualize it.

hierarchy.lvl1: NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine
NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine

records.content: Sentinel-2 is a high-resolution remote sensing satellite with multiple spectral bands that can be used for various analyses, including land cover identification and water monitoring. In this analysis, we will use Sentinel-2 imagery with atmospheric correction (COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED).

hierarchy.lvl1: NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine
hierarchy.lvl2: Data Processing in Google Earth Engine

hierarchy.lvl1: NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine
hierarchy.lvl2: Data Processing in Google Earth Engine

records.content: Here are the steps for processing Sentinel-2 data in Google Earth Engine:

hierarchy.lvl1: NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine
NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine

records.content:
var sentinel2 = ee.ImageCollection('COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED')

  .filterDate('2024-01-01', '2025-01-01')

  .filter(ee.Filter.lt('CLOUDY_PIXEL_PERCENTAGE', 20))

  .map(function(img) { return img.updateMask(img.select('QA60').eq(0)); })

  .median().clip(table).multiply(0.0001);

This code performs:

Retrieving Sentinel-2 data within a one-year period (2024–01–01 to 2025–01–01)

Filtering images with cloud cover below 20%.

Removing cloud effects using the QA60 band.

Taking the median value of the remaining images and clipping it to the study area.

hierarchy.lvl1: NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine
NDWI Analysis Using Sentinel-2 in Google Earth Engine

records.content: NDWI is calculated using the formula: NDWI=Green−NIRGreen+NIRNDWI = \frac{Green — NIR}{Green + NIR} In Sentinel-2, the green band is B3, and the Near-Infrared (NIR) band is B8. Implementation in GEE:var NDWI = sentinel2.normalizedDifference(['B3', 'B8']).rename('NDWI');

records.content:
Positive values (close to 1) indicate water bodies such as rivers, lakes, or wetlands.

Negative values indicate non-water areas such as dry land and vegetation.

Values close to zero typically indicate moist land or areas with low water content.

records.content:
Using Google Earth Engine, we can easily calculate and visualize NDWI from Sentinel-2 imagery. This analysis is highly useful for water resource monitoring, wetland change detection, and other environmental management applications.

What’s next? If you are interested in further analysis, you can try other indices such as NDVI for vegetation analysis or MNDWI for more accurate water identification. Happy coding!

records.content:

Semua tulisan

Oleh : Defani Arman A

Dalam analisis spektral, banyak platform tersedia, namun saya memilih R karena bersifat open-source, kuat dalam analisis data spasial, serta didukung oleh banyak paket seperti raster, terra, dan sf. Selain itu, R memungkinkan integrasi langsung antara statistik, visualisasi, dan pengolahan citra satelit dalam satu lingkungan kerja.

Seri ini saya buat untuk membantu memahami konsep dasar analisis spektral menggunakan R, dimulai dari perhitungan NDVI, salah satu indeks vegetasi paling umum dalam penginderaan jauh.

hierarchy.lvl1: Penginderaan Jarak Jauh Dasar Menggunakan Bahasa R | Analisis NDVI Citra Satelit Sentinel 2A
Penginderaan Jarak Jauh Dasar Menggunakan Bahasa R | Analisis NDVI Citra Satelit Sentinel 2A

records.content:
NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) adalah salah satu indeks vegetasi paling populer dalam penginderaan jauh yang digunakan untuk memantau kondisi dan kerapatan vegetasi di permukaan bumi. Indeks ini diciptakan oleh Rouse et al. pada tahun 1973 melalui penelitian legendaris yang berjudul “Monitoring Vegetation Systems in the Great Plains with ERTS” di Texas A&M University. Dalam penelitian tersebut, Rouse dan timnya memanfaatkan data satelit ERTS‑1 (kemudian dikenal sebagai Landsat‑1) untuk memantau rangeland di kawasan Great Plains, Amerika Serikat. Mereka mengembangkan sebuah metode kuantitatif untuk mengukur kondisi vegetasi dengan menggunakan rasio pantulan antara panjang gelombang inframerah dekat (NIR) dan merah (Red). Hasil penelitian itu menunjukkan bahwa rasio ini sangat berkorelasi dengan biomassa hijau di atas permukaan tanah dan kelembapan vegetasi, sehingga dapat menjadi indikator efektif kondisi vegetasi secara regional.

Secara matematis, NDVI dirumuskan sebagai:

NDVI = (Near Infrared-Red)/(Near Infrared+Red)

di mana NIR adalah nilai pantulan pada band inframerah dekat dan RED adalah nilai pantulan pada band merah. Nilai NDVI berkisar antara –1 hingga +1. Nilai mendekati +1 menunjukkan vegetasi sehat dan lebat karena tanaman sehat memantulkan banyak cahaya inframerah dekat dan menyerap banyak cahaya merah untuk fotosintesis. Nilai mendekati 0 biasanya menunjukkan tanah terbuka atau area dengan vegetasi jarang, sedangkan nilai negatif mengindikasikan badan air atau objek non‑vegetasi.

Dalam konteks citra Sentinel‑2 yang digunakan dalam contoh ini, NDVI dihitung dengan memanfaatkan Band 8 (Near Infrared) sebagai NIR dan Band 4 (Red) sebagai RED. Kedua band ini sudah disimpan dalam format GeoTIFF (.tif) dan siap diproses di R. Berkat kesederhanaannya, NDVI hingga saat ini tetap menjadi indeks dasar yang digunakan luas dalam kehutanan, pertanian, pemantauan lahan, dan berbagai bidang lain yang membutuhkan informasi cepat dan akurat mengenai kondisi vegetasi.

Nilai NDVI pada setiap tipe objek di bumi (Rizvi et al., 2009)

records.content:
Dalam dunia penginderaan jauh, data citra satelit umumnya disimpan dalam format raster, yaitu kumpulan grid piksel yang merepresentasikan nilai reflektansi atau intensitas dari permukaan bumi. Setiap piksel menyimpan angka yang dapat diolah menjadi informasi, misalnya untuk memetakan vegetasi, permukaan air, atau penggunaan lahan. Untuk memproses data jenis ini di R, komunitas geospasial mengandalkan sebuah package penting bernama raster.

Package raster dikembangkan oleh Robert J. Hijmans sebagai penulis utama sekaligus maintainer, dengan kontribusi dari banyak pakar lain seperti Jacob van Etten, Michael Sumner, Joe Cheng, Dan Baston, Andrew Bevan, Roger Bivand, Lorenzo Busetto, Mort Canty, dan masih banyak lagi. Sejak awal pengembangannya sekitar tahun 2010, raster terus berevolusi dan menjadi standar de facto untuk analisis data raster di lingkungan R. Versi yang tercatat pada dokumentasi terbaru adalah versi 3.6‑32, yang dirilis di CRAN pada 28 Maret 2025, menandakan bahwa pengembangannya tetap aktif dan relevan hingga kini.

Tujuan dibuatnya package ini adalah untuk membaca, menulis, memanipulasi, menganalisis, dan memodelkan data raster secara efisien, bahkan untuk data dengan ukuran sangat besar yang tidak dapat dimuat sepenuhnya ke memori. Package ini menyediakan kelas objek seperti RasterLayer, RasterStack, dan RasterBrick untuk mengelola data raster tunggal maupun multi‑band. Dengan raster, pengguna dapat melakukan operasi matematika antar layer (dikenal sebagai raster algebra), mengubah resolusi atau proyeksi, melakukan cropping dan masking, menghitung statistik seperti rata‑rata atau histogram, serta membuat peta tematik dengan fungsi plot() atau plotRGB().

Meskipun saat ini sudah tersedia package penerus bernama terra yang lebih modern, raster tetap banyak digunakan karena dokumentasinya yang sangat lengkap, kompatibilitasnya dengan berbagai tutorial lama, dan komunitas pengguna yang besar. Tidak heran jika raster menjadi langkah awal yang tepat untuk mempelajari dasar‑dasar penginderaan jauh menggunakan Bahasa R, sebelum nantinya beralih ke package yang lebih baru seperti terra.

Setelah proses instalasi selesai, setiap kali memulai sesi baru di RStudio kita harus memanggil package ini ke memori dengan menggunakan perintah library(raster). Langkah ini wajib dilakukan agar fungsi‑fungsi seperti raster(), plot(), atau operasi aljabar raster dapat digunakan tanpa menimbulkan error. Dengan selesainya tahap instalasi dan pemanggilan package, maka lingkungan kerja R sudah siap untuk membaca dan mengolah data raster.install.packages("raster")

records.content:
Setelah package raster berhasil diinstal dan dimuat, tahap berikutnya adalah membaca data raster yang sudah diunduh. Pada contoh ini digunakan data Sentinel‑2 dengan dua band utama yang diperlukan untuk perhitungan NDVI, yaitu Band 8 (NIR) dan Band 4 (Red). Kedua file tersebut sudah disimpan di komputer dalam format GeoTIFF (.tif) dengan nama B8.tif untuk Band 8 dan B4.tif untuk Band 4. Berikut potongan kode untuk memanggilnya di R:NIR <- raster("D:/R/B8.tif")

RED <- raster("D:/R/B4.tif")

Memanggil data raster (Sumber : Tangkapan Layar)

Penjelasan tiap bagian kode:

raster() → Fungsi dari package raster untuk membaca file raster dari direktori lokal.

“D:/R/B8.tif” → Path lengkap file Band 8 (Near Infrared/NIR) Sentinel‑2 dalam format GeoTIFF.

“D:/R/B4.tif” → Path lengkap file Band 4 (Red) Sentinel‑2 dalam format GeoTIFF.

<- → Operator assignment yang menyimpan hasil pembacaan ke variabel di sebelah kiri.

NIR → Variabel untuk menyimpan objek raster hasil pembacaan Band 8 (NIR).

RED → Variabel untuk menyimpan objek raster hasil pembacaan Band 4 (Red).

Setelah kedua perintah ini dijalankan, objek NIR dan RED sudah tersedia di memori R dan siap untuk diolah lebih lanjut. Tahap ini sangat penting karena menjadi dasar dari setiap perhitungan berikutnya. Dengan memuat band NIR dan Red ke dalam R, kita telah menyiapkan data yang diperlukan untuk perhitungan NDVI, yang akan dibahas pada subbab selanjutnya. Meskipun pada langkah ini kita belum melakukan perhitungan apa pun, memastikan bahwa data sudah terbaca dengan benar adalah kunci utama untuk mencegah kesalahan di proses berikutnya.

records.content:
etelah data raster Band 8 (NIR) dan Band 4 (Red) dari Sentinel‑2 berhasil dibaca, langkah berikutnya adalah menghitung NDVI menggunakan operasi aljabar raster. Package raster memungkinkan kita melakukan operasi matematika langsung di antara dua objek raster, sehingga perhitungan NDVI dapat ditulis dengan sangat sederhana. Berikut kode yang digunakan:NDVI <- (NIR-RED)/(NIR+RED)

Menghitung NDVI (Sumber : Tangkapan Layar)

Penjelasan kode:

NIR - RED menghitung selisih nilai piksel antara Band 8 (Near Infrared) dan Band 4 (Red).

NIR + RED menghitung jumlah nilai piksel antara kedua band.

/ membagi hasil selisih dengan hasil jumlah untuk setiap piksel, sehingga menghasilkan nilai NDVI.

NDVI adalah variabel baru yang menyimpan hasil raster NDVI.

Pada tahap ini, kita sudah memiliki objek raster NDVI di memori R yang siap digunakan untuk berbagai analisis lebih lanjut.

records.content:
Setelah NDVI selesai dihitung, kita dapat memvisualisasikannya menjadi peta tematik sehingga lebih mudah dipahami. Package raster menyediakan fungsi plot() yang dapat langsung digunakan untuk menampilkan raster di jendela grafis. Kita juga dapat menambahkan judul dengan parameter main untuk memberi keterangan pada peta. Untuk menjalankan semua kode dilakukan dengan menekan tombol “run” atau dengan ctrl + A lalu tekan “enter” . Berikut contohnya:plot(NDVI, main = "Normalized Difference Vegetation Index")

Menampilkan Visualisasi NDVI (Sumber : Tangkapan Layar)

Penjelasan kode:

plot(NDVI) memanggil fungsi untuk menampilkan raster NDVI sebagai peta.

main = “Normalized Difference Vegetation Index” menambahkan judul pada peta agar pembaca peta tahu bahwa yang ditampilkan adalah hasil NDVI.

Hasil visualisasi akan menampilkan peta dengan rentang nilai NDVI dari –1 hingga +1. Warna pada peta menunjukkan variasi nilai NDVI di seluruh area citra. Nilai mendekati +1 tampak pada area dengan vegetasi sehat, nilai mendekati 0 menunjukkan area dengan vegetasi jarang atau tanah terbuka, sedangkan nilai negatif umumnya terlihat pada area perairan atau objek non‑vegetasi. Visualisasi akan tampil sebagai berikut

Plot NDVI dalam antarmuka R Studio (Sumber : Tangkapan Layar)

Menyimpan Hasil NDVI dalam format “GeoTIFF)

Setelah NDVI dihitung dan divisualisasikan, kita sering kali memerlukan penyimpanan hasil dalam bentuk file baru agar dapat digunakan kembali tanpa perlu menghitung ulang. Package raster menyediakan fungsi writeRaster() untuk menyimpan objek raster ke berbagai format file, termasuk GeoTIFF (.tif) yang umum digunakan dalam aplikasi GIS. Menyimpan hasil NDVI juga berguna ketika kita ingin membagikannya kepada orang lain atau menggunakannya di perangkat lunak GIS lain seperti QGIS atau ArcGIS. Berikut contoh kode untuk menyimpan NDVI ke dalam file GeoTIFF:writeRaster(NDVI, "D:/R/NDVI.tif", format = "GTiff", overwrite = TRUE)

Penjelasan kode:

✅ NDVI adalah objek raster yang akan disimpan.

✅ “D:/R/NDVI.tif” adalah lokasi dan nama file output yang dihasilkan.

✅ format = “GTiff” memastikan file disimpan sebagai GeoTIFF.

✅ overwrite = TRUE memperbolehkan file lama dengan nama yang sama untuk ditimpa.

Setelah perintah ini dijalankan, file NDVI.tif akan muncul di direktori yang dituju. File tersebut dapat langsung dibuka di perangkat lunak GIS atau diolah kembali dalam sesi R berikutnya. Dengan demikian, hasil analisismu tidak hanya tampil di layar tetapi juga tersimpan sebagai file yang bisa digunakan kapan saja.

Selain menyimpan hasil NDVI sebagai file raster (GeoTIFF), sering kali kita juga ingin menyimpan tampilan peta NDVI yang sudah divisualisasikan ke dalam bentuk gambar. Format PNG sangat umum digunakan untuk laporan, presentasi, atau publikasi karena ringan, mendukung transparansi, dan mudah dibagikan.

Di R, kita bisa menggunakan fungsi png() untuk membuka perangkat grafis PNG, lalu memanggil fungsi plot() untuk membuat peta, dan terakhir menggunakan dev.off() untuk menutup perangkat dan menyimpan file gambar. Berikut contohnya:png("D:/R/NDVI_layout.png", width = 1200, height = 1000, res = 150)



plot(NDVI, main = "Normalized Difference Vegetation Index")



dev.off()

Penjelasan kode:

png(“D:/R/NDVI_layout.png”) membuka perangkat grafis untuk menulis output ke file PNG dengan nama NDVI_layout.png di folder D:/R/.

width dan height mengatur ukuran gambar dalam piksel, sedangkan res mengatur resolusi (dpi) untuk hasil yang tajam.

plot(NDVI, main = “...”) menampilkan peta NDVI, outputnya akan langsung diarahkan ke file PNG.

dev.off() menutup perangkat grafis, langkah ini wajib dilakukan agar file PNG benar‑benar tersimpan.

records.content:
Digital Elevation Model (DEM) adalah data raster yang menyimpan informasi ketinggian permukaan bumi pada setiap pikselnya. DEM banyak dimanfaatkan dalam bidang kehutanan, konservasi, tata guna lahan, hingga mitigasi bencana. Dari DEM, kita dapat menghitung parameter turunan seperti slope (kemiringan lereng), aspect (arah lereng), dan hillshade (efek bayangan permukaan) yang memudahkan interpretasi topografi.

Salah satu perangkat lunak yang populer untuk analisis data spasial adalah R. Di R, tersedia paket terra yang dirancang khusus untuk memproses dan menganalisis data raster maupun vektor secara efisien. Paket terra dikembangkan oleh Robert J. Hijmans (University of California, Davis) sebagai penerus dari paket raster dengan kinerja yang lebih baik dan dukungan terhadap format data modern. Dokumentasi resminya tersedia di 

https://​CRAN​.R​-project​.org​/package​=​terra.

records.content: Curah hujan merupakan salah satu parameter iklim fundamental yang memengaruhi berbagai sektor, mulai dari hidrologi, pertanian, hingga mitigasi bencana. Analisis curah hujan dalam agregat tahunan memberikan gambaran umum mengenai kondisi basah atau kering suatu wilayah selama satu periode. Platform Google Earth Engine (GEE) menyediakan kapabilitas komputasi awan untuk pemrosesan data geospasial berskala besar. Penelitian ini mendemonstrasikan alur kerja untuk akuisisi, pengolahan, dan visualisasi data curah hujan tahunan menggunakan koleksi data CHIRPS Daily dalam lingkungan GEE, studi kasus di Kabupaten Ciamis, Indonesia. Alur kerja ini mencakup pembuatan legenda kartografis kustom untuk interpretasi data yang lebih informatif.

records.content:
Curah hujan tahunan didefinisikan sebagai total presipitasi (dalam satuan milimeter) yang terakumulasi di suatu lokasi selama satu tahun kalender. Data ini krusial untuk pemodelan neraca air hidrologis, perencanaan agrikultur terkait penentuan pola tanam, serta sebagai indikator awal untuk analisis potensi kekeringan maupun banjir (Dore, 2005).

Untuk melakukan analisis tersebut, diperlukan data curah hujan yang memiliki konsistensi temporal dan resolusi spasial yang memadai. Salah satu produk data yang paling sering digunakan dalam komunitas ilmiah adalah CHIRPS.

records.content:
CHIRPS adalah dataset presipitasi quasi-global (mencakup 50°S — 50°N) yang dikembangkan oleh Climate Hazards Group di University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) bekerja sama dengan U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Earth Resources Observation and Science (EROS) Center.

Dataset ini memiliki beberapa keunggulan utama:

Resolusi Spasial Tinggi: CHIRPS menyediakan data dengan resolusi spasial 0.05° (sekitar 5.3 km), yang sangat detail untuk analisis skala regional maupun lokal.

Periode Data Panjang: Data tersedia dari tahun 1981 hingga mendekati waktu-nyata (near real-time), memungkinkan analisis tren jangka panjang.

Metodologi Hibrida: CHIRPS mengintegrasikan data satelit inframerah (InfraRed — IR) dari citra Cold Cloud Duration (CCD) dengan data observasi dari stasiun-stasiun cuaca di seluruh dunia. Pendekatan ini menghasilkan estimasi curah hujan yang lebih akurat dibandingkan jika hanya menggunakan satu sumber data (Funk et al., 2015).

Data ini dapat diakses secara bebas melalui katalog data Google Earth Engine dengan ID: UCSB-CHG/CHIRPS/DAILY.

records.content:
Wilayah studi didefinisikan sebagai batas administrasi Provinsi Jawa Barat. Data batas wilayah ini diekstraksi dari dataset FAO Global Administrative Unit Layers (GAUL) level 1, yang merepresentasikan entitas provinsi.var aoi = ee.FeatureCollection('FAO/GAUL/2015/level1')

  .filter(ee.Filter.eq('ADM1_NAME', 'Jawa Barat'))

  .geometry();

ee.FeatureCollection(‘FAO/GAUL/2015/level1’): Fungsi ini memuat sebuah koleksi data vektor global dari Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Dataset GAUL (Global Administrative Unit Layers) level 1 ini berisi batas-batas administrasi tingkat provinsi atau negara bagian di seluruh dunia.

.filter(ee.Filter.eq(‘ADM1_NAME’, ‘Jawa Barat’)): Setelah seluruh data provinsi dimuat, fungsi .filter() diterapkan untuk menyaringnya. Filter ini mencari fitur (poligon) yang memiliki kolom atribut (properti) bernama ADM1_NAME dengan nilai yang sama persis (eq atau equals) dengan “Jawa Barat”. Hasilnya adalah sebuah FeatureCollection yang hanya berisi satu fitur, yaitu poligon Provinsi Jawa Barat.

.geometry(): Fungsi ini mengekstrak hanya informasi spasial (yaitu, bentuk poligonnya) dari fitur yang telah disaring dan mengabaikan semua data atribut lainnya (seperti nama, kode, dll.). Hasil akhir yang disimpan dalam variabel aoi adalah sebuah objek geometri poligon murni.

ee.ImageCollection(“UCSB-CHG/CHIRPS/DAILY”): Memuat seluruh koleksi citra satelit CHIRPS Daily. Ini adalah kumpulan data time-series yang berisi ribuan citra, di mana setiap citra merepresentasikan estimasi curah hujan global untuk satu hari.

.filter(

ee.Filter.date(‘2023-01-01’, ‘2023-12-31’)): Menyaring koleksi citra raksasa tersebut untuk mengambil hanya citra yang tanggal akuisisinya berada dalam rentang 1 Januari 2023 hingga 31 Desember 2023. Hasilnya adalah 365 citra (untuk tahun tersebut).

.sum(): Fungsi ini melakukan operasi matematika penting. Ia “menumpuk” ke-365 citra harian tersebut dan menjumlahkan nilai piksel di setiap lokasi. Hasilnya adalah satu citra tunggal (ee.Image) di mana setiap nilai pikselnya merepresentasikan total curah hujan tahunan dalam satuan milimeter.

.clip(aoi): Memotong citra hasil penjumlahan tadi menggunakan poligon aoi sebagai “cetakan”. Semua data piksel yang berada di luar batas Provinsi Jawa Barat akan dibuang, sehingga menghasilkan citra curah hujan yang hanya mencakup wilayah studi.

23 November 2025 · Terbit pertama di 

Medium · 

Semua tulisan

Oleh: Defani Arman Alfitriansyah

Pendahuluan

Ekosistem mangrove merupakan salah satu ekosistem pesisir paling produktif yang menyimpan stok karbon sangat besar dalam biomassa pohon, bahan organik tanah, dan sedimen sebagai karbon biru yang berkontribusi pada mitigasi perubahan iklim global (Hossain et al., 2025). Indonesia memiliki luasan mangrove mencapai 3,329,459.72 hektare pada tahun 2018 yang tersebar di Pulau Papua, Sulawesi, Kalimantan, Sumatera, dan Jawa, namun menghadapi tekanan antropogenik berkelanjutan dari ekspansi akuakultur, konversi lahan, dan pembangunan infrastruktur yang mengakibatkan degradasi ekosistem (Gunawan et al., 2025). Pemantauan spasial dan temporal stok karbon mangrove menjadi kritis untuk mendukung kebijakan perubahan iklim nasional dan pengembangan pasar karbon sukarela (Roy et al., 2024).

Metode konvensional estimasi biomassa dan stok karbon mangrove mengandalkan pengukuran lapangan intensif yang memiliki keterbatasan cakupan spasial terbatas, biaya operasional tinggi, dan kesulitan akses ke daerah terpencil (Ullah et al., 2025). Teknologi penginderaan jauh satelit telah terbukti menjadi alat berharga untuk pemantauan mangrove dalam skala besar dengan biaya operasional lebih rendah (Aransiola et al., 2026). Berbagai indeks vegetasi berbasis satelit telah dikembangkan untuk estimasi stok karbon mangrove, mencakup Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index (SAVI), dan Mangrove Index (MI) (Purnomo Aji et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024). Studi sebelumnya menunjukkan bahwa indeks vegetasi memiliki kemampuan bervariasi dalam mengidentifikasi mangrove dan mengestimasi hubungan karakteristik spektral dengan variabel struktural hutan seperti biomassa (Wu et al., 2025). Namun, penggunaan indeks vegetasi tunggal atau data sensor tunggal menghasilkan akurasi estimasi terbatas, terutama menghadapi variabilitas spektral tinggi akibat perbedaan spesies mangrove, struktur hutan beragam, dan pengaruh pasang surut signifikan terhadap pantulan spektral (Winarso et al., 2023).

Strategi integrasi data multisensor menggabungkan informasi dari berbagai platform penginderaan jauh, termasuk data optik multispektral (Sentinel-2 dan Landsat 8), data radar sintetis apertur (Sentinel-1 dan ALOS PALSAR-2), dan data LiDAR spasial (ICESat-2 dan GEDI) untuk menghasilkan estimasi karbon lebih akurat dan komprehensif (Pradisty et al., 2025; Simarmata et al., 2025). Penelitian terbaru menunjukkan kombinasi data optik dan SAR meningkatkan akurasi estimasi stok karbon mangrove hingga 90 persen atau lebih dibandingkan sensor tunggal, karena data optik memberikan informasi spektral dan indeks vegetasi, sementara data SAR memberikan informasi struktur biomassa unik (Chen et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025). Algoritma pembelajaran mesin seperti Random Forest, Gradient Tree Boosting, dan neural network ensemble menunjukkan performa superior dalam menangani hubungan non-linier kompleks antara variabel spektral/SAR dan stok karbon mangrove, memberikan estimasi robust terhadap variasi lokal dan temporal (Febrianto et al., 2025; Simarmata et al., 2025). Platform komputasi cloud seperti Google Earth Engine membuat akses dan pemrosesan data satelit lebih mudah dan efisien, memungkinkan analisis multisensor dalam skala besar ( Wu et al., 2025).

Meskipun kemajuan signifikan telah dicapai, celah penelitian substansial masih ada (Roy et al., 2024). Pertama, standarisasi metodologi untuk estimasi karbon mangrove pada tingkat spesies masih belum sepenuhnya tercapai, mengingat berbagai spesies mangrove menunjukkan karakteristik spektral dan struktural berbeda (Hidayatullah et al., 2023). Kedua, estimasi karbon bawah permukaan tanah masih kurang dikaji intensif dibandingkan biomassa di atas permukaan, padahal komponen bawah tanah dapat menyimpan karbon sama atau lebih besar (Xie et al., 2025). Ketiga, penelitian dinamika temporal stok karbon mangrove masih terbatas geografis dengan keterwakilan tidak merata (Mohan et al., 2025). Diperlukan pengembangan metodologi multisensor inovatif, algoritma pembelajaran mesin lebih canggih, dan validasi lapangan komprehensif untuk meningkatkan akurasi estimasi karbon mangrove pada skala regional dan global (Roy et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025).

30 November 2025 · Terbit pertama di 

Medium · 

Semua tulisan

Defani Arman Alfitriansyah

Alur Kerja Klasifikasi Citra (Dibuat menggunakan notebook lm)

A. Pendahuluan

Penginderaan jauh satelit menjadi instrumen utama dalam pemantauan dinamika Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) secara global dan berkelanjutan, karena mampu menyediakan informasi spasial-temporal yang konsisten untuk mendukung pemodelan iklim, pengelolaan banjir, perencanaan kota, dan mitigasi perubahan iklim (Ganjirad & Bagheri, 2024; Gorelick et al., 2017; Alshehri et al., 2025).

Ketersediaan data open-access beresolusi tinggi seperti Sentinel-2 MSI (10–20 m) dan Landsat 8 OLI, dikombinasikan dengan platform cloud computing Google Earth Engine (GEE), telah mengubah cara pengolahan citra skala besar menjadi cepat, murah, dan dapat direproduksi tanpa infrastruktur lokal (Gorelick et al., 2017; Abdollahi et al., 2023; Alshehri et al., 2025). GEE memungkinkan akses langsung ke data surface reflectance yang telah terkoreksi atmosfer serta komputasi paralel skala planet, sehingga menjadi platform dominan untuk pemetaan LULC di berbagai wilayah tropis dan subtropis (Chowdhury, 2023; Sharma et al., 2025).

Awan dan bayangan awan merupakan gangguan utama pada citra optik di wilayah tropis, sehingga langkah cloud masking yang andal menjadi prasyarat mutlak untuk menghasilkan komposit citra berkualitas tinggi (Kosasih et al., 2019). Sentinel-2 menyediakan Scene Classification Layer (SCL) yang secara spesifik mendeteksi awan, cirrus, dan bayangan awan, sehingga memungkinkan pembentukan komposit median tahunan yang bersih. Pengayaan fitur dengan indeks spektral (NDVI, SAVI, NDWI, NDMI, NDBI, MVI) serta integrasi data topografi NASADEM (elevasi dan kemiringan lereng) terbukti sangat efektif meningkatkan separabilitas kelas pada lanskap heterogen seperti daerah aliran sungai, perkotaan, dan perbukitan (Rouse et al., 1974; Huete, 1988; McFeeters, 1996; Gao, 1996; Zha et al., 2003; Buckley et al., 2020; Abdollahi et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2025).

Tutorial ini bertujuan memberikan panduan lengkap dan praktis untuk memetakan LULC menggunakan Sentinel-2 tahun 2024–2025 di Google Earth Engine dengan algoritma Random Forest. Langkah-langkah yang akan dibahas secara berurutan meliputi: cloud masking berbasis SCL, pembuatan komposit median tahunan, perhitungan indeks spektral, integrasi data NASADEM (elevasi dan slope), pelatihan serta penerapan model Random Forest, dan ekspor peta LULC akhir dalam format GeoTIFF siap paka

B. Kajian Pustaka

Random Forest

Algoritma Random Forest (RF) yang diperkenalkan oleh Breiman (2001) merupakan metode ensemble learning berbasis decision tree yang hingga saat ini tetap menjadi salah satu klasifier paling populer dan robust dalam pemetaan tutupan lahan berbasis penginderaan jauh (Belgiu & Drăguţ, 2016; Maxwell et al., 2018). RF bekerja dengan membangun ratusan hingga ribuan pohon keputusan (decision trees) secara paralel, di mana setiap pohon dilatih pada subset acak sampel pelatihan (bootstrap aggregating atau bagging) dan subset acak fitur pada setiap percabangan (random feature selection). Hasil akhir diperoleh melalui voting mayoritas (untuk klasifikasi) atau rata-rata prediksi (untuk regresi), sehingga mengurangi overfitting dan meningkatkan stabilitas model.

Konsep Algoritma Random Forest (Chardile et al., 2024)

Keunggulan RF dalam konteks klasifikasi tutupan lahan telah terbukti secara konsisten pada berbagai tipe citra dan lanskap. Ganjirad dan Bagheri (2024) menggunakan RF pada Google Earth Engine untuk menghasilkan peta LULC berbasis skema USGS 24-kelas dari citra Landsat 8, menunjukkan bahwa RF secara signifikan mengungguli CART, Gradient Tree Boosting, dan SVM, terutama ketika dikombinasikan dengan pendekatan object-based dan fitur musiman. Sharma et al. (2025) pada citra LISS-4 di wilayah sungai Mahanadi-Shivnath juga menyimpulkan bahwa RF dengan fitur spektral + indeks + topografi memberikan performa terbaik dibandingkan SVM dan Gradient Tree Boosting, khususnya dalam mendelineasi saluran air sempit dan vegetasi jarang.

Studi perkotaan oleh Chowdhury (2023) di Dhaka membandingkan RF, SVM, ANN, dan Maximum Likelihood; hasil menunjukkan RF mencapai overall accuracy 94% dan Kappa 0.91, hanya sedikit di bawah ANN (95% dan 0.93), tetapi jauh lebih stabil dan tidak memerlukan tuning hiperparameter yang rumit. Abdollahi et al. (2023) di Melbourne metropolitan menggunakan RF pada 80 citra Landsat-8 multitemporal di GEE dan mencatat bahwa RF mampu menangani data berdimensi tinggi (spektral + indeks + topografi) dengan baik, menghasilkan overall accuracy 88,47% sebelum post-processing dan meningkat menjadi 92,90% setelah penghilangan salt-and-pepper noise.

Keandalan RF juga terlihat pada aplikasi skala nasional dan global. Meta-analisis oleh Alshehri et al. (2025) terhadap 72 publikasi GEE-LULC (2016–Februari 2025) menunjukkan bahwa Random Forest adalah algoritma yang paling sering digunakan (frekuensi tertinggi bersama SVM), terutama karena kemampuannya menangani data tidak linear, tidak memerlukan asumsi distribusi normal, serta menyediakan informasi feature importance yang berguna untuk interpretasi ekologis.

Beberapa penelitian juga menegaskan bahwa RF relatif tidak sensitif terhadap noise dan ketidakseimbangan kelas, serta memiliki waktu komputasi yang efisien pada platform cloud seperti GEE (Gorelick et al., 2017; Abdollahi et al., 2023). Oleh karena itu, RF dipilih sebagai algoritma utama dalam tutorial ini karena keseimbangan antara performa tinggi, kemudahan implementasi, dan interpretabilitas hasil pada data Sentinel-2 yang kompleks.

2. NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index)

Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) merupakan indeks vegetasi paling fundamental dan paling banyak digunakan dalam penginderaan jauh sejak diperkenalkan oleh Rouse et al. (1974). NDVI memanfaatkan kontras reflektansi yang sangat tinggi antara kanal near-infrared (NIR) dan red pada vegetasi hijau yang sehat, di mana klorofil menyerap cahaya merah secara kuat untuk fotosintesis, sedangkan struktur sel daun menyebarkan cahaya NIR secara intensif. Rumus NDVI adalah sebagai berikut:

NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red)

di mana:

NIR = reflektansi kanal near-infrared (Sentinel-2 Band 8, 842 nm), Red = reflektansi kanal red (Sentinel-2 Band 4, 665 nm)

Nilai NDVI berkisar antara −1 hingga +1. Nilai negatif umumnya menunjukkan permukaan air atau awan, nilai mendekati 0 menunjukkan tanah terbuka atau vegetasi sangat jarang, sedangkan nilai tinggi (0,6–0,9) mengindikasikan vegetasi hijau yang lebat dan sehat (Rouse et al., 1974; Ganjirad & Bagheri, 2024).

NDVI telah terbukti menjadi fitur yang sangat penting dalam klasifikasi tutupan lahan berbasis machine learning. Ganjirad dan Bagheri (2024) menunjukkan bahwa NDVI menjadi salah satu dari tiga fitur terpenting dalam model Random Forest untuk skema USGS 24-kelas. Abdollahi et al. (2023) serta Sharma et al. (2025) juga secara konsisten menempatkan NDVI pada peringkat pertama atau kedua dalam feature importance ketika dikombinasikan dengan indeks lain dan data topografi. Meskipun NDVI dapat mengalami saturasi pada kanopi sangat lebat (LAI > 3) dan sensitif terhadap kecerahan tanah pada vegetasi jarang, kombinasi dengan indeks penyesuai tanah seperti SAVI atau integrasi multitemporal tetap menjadikannya fitur esensial dalam klasifikasi LULC modern (Huete, 1988; Alshehri et al., 2025). Oleh karena itu, NDVI akan selalu disertakan sebagai salah satu band input utama dalam tutorial ini untuk memastikan separabilitas kelas vegetasi yang optimal pada citra Sentinel-2.

Saat ini saya bekerja di bidang agroforestri, membangun basis data GIS dan sistem WebGIS untuk mendukung pengelolaan data spasial, pemantauan, dan ketelusuran (traceability). Apa harus install software berbayar?

Tidak. GeoLibre dan DuckDB gratis dan open source.

Saya belum pernah ngoding sama sekali, bisa?

Bisa. Buku ini mulai dari nol, termasuk menjelaskan apa itu query.

Datanya dari mana?

RBI dari Badan Informasi Geospasial, tuplah, batas TNGC, dan batas wilayah Jawa Barat. Semua sudah disiapkan di folder Google Drive.

Bisa dipakai di HP?

EPUB-nya enak dibaca di HP. Untuk praktek tetap butuh laptop.

Yang perlu disiapkan: laptop Windows, macOS, atau Linux, dan GeoLibre Desktop (gratis). Tidak perlu jago coding.

Produk digital, file dikirim otomatis setelah pembayaran. Buku ini panduan independen dan tidak berafiliasi resmi dengan proyek GeoLibre atau DuckDB.

Modul penginderaan jauh yang bisa diakses dan diunduh gratis dari Google Drive.

I’m a Forestry graduate specializing in remote sensing, forest carbon modeling, ecological modeling, and cloud-based geospatial technology for environmental applications.

I’m now working in agroforestry, building GIS databases and WebGIS systems to support spatial data management, monitoring, and traceability. My work covers developing spatial datasets, processing and analyzing geospatial data, and producing maps and visualizations that support forest and environmental decision-making.

My research background centers on forest carbon assessment, biomass modeling, and Sentinel-2 spectral analysis, using 

Google Earth Engine and an open-source 

Python ecosystem (

pandas,

I also serve as a GIS & Spatial Modeling Laboratory Assistant, mentoring students in GIS, remote sensing, Google Earth Engine, and Python-based spatial analysis.

I build open-source geospatial tools: RasterViz, a QGIS plugin for Matplotlib-style raster visualization without coding, used by 1,300+ users worldwide, and the GeoLibre plugins Layout Composer, GBIF Data and iNaturalist Extractor.

As a content creator on Instagram (

@49s.lab, 6K+ followers), I share practical GIS, remote sensing, and open-source geospatial tutorials. I work with open-source software only, and I’m open to collaboration on forest carbon, sustainability, EUDR, and GIS-based traceability systems.

records.content:
Learn spatial SQL from scratch in plain language, practising in GeoLibre, which is free and open source. The book is written in Indonesian.

Rp85,000 · Ebook PDF + EPUB · 420 pages

Buy on Mayar · 

Read a sample

A relaxed, Indonesian-language ebook that teaches vector data processing with DuckDB SQL inside GeoLibre: from installing GeoLibre and the SQL Workspace to case studies on clipping official land cover data, carbon stock in Mount Ciremai National Park, and biodiversity indices from GBIF and iNaturalist. All exercises use real data from Kuningan Regency and West Java, with sample data ready to download.

Downloading, installing and updating GeoLibre, and what its MIT licence means

A tour of GeoLibre’s menus, with their QGIS equivalents

Preparing data: converting the official RBI topographic data to GeoJSON and GeoParquet

SQL basics: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, CASE, JOIN, CTE, window functions

Spatial SQL: coordinate systems and UTM, area, length, distance, spatial join, buffer, clip, dissolve

Case studies: land cover in Kuningan, carbon stock in Mount Ciremai National Park, biodiversity from GBIF and iNaturalist

420 pages, 4 parts, 26 chapters

155 figures and screenshots of the latest GeoLibre

147 SQL examples with syntax highlighting

This notebook demonstrates the implementation of the Automatic Mangrove Map and Index (AMMI) algorithm using Python-based geospatial tools on Google Earth Engine (GEE).

Repositori di GitHub

Based on: Suyarso & Avianto (2022) | Platform: Google Earth Engine + Python

This notebook demonstrates the implementation of the Automatic Mangrove Map and Index (AMMI) algorithm using Python-based geospatial tools on Google Earth Engine (GEE). The workflow encompasses cloud-masked Sentinel-2 imagery compositing, AMMI index computation, mangrove binary classification, and canopy density visualization — all rendered as publication-quality static maps using cartoee.

The AMMI algorithm was developed specifically for mangrove ecosystems and has been validated in Indonesian coastal settings, including the Aru Islands and the Musi River Delta, South Sumatra (Suyarso, 2022; Suyarso & Avianto, 2022).

Prepared by: Defani Arman Alfitriansyah — Faculty of Forestry, Universitas Kuningan

Scientific Background

AMMI Formula and Thresholds

Dependencies

Data and Region of Interest

Workflow Summary

Code Walkthrough

References

Mangrove forests occupy the intertidal zones of tropical and subtropical coastlines and provide critical ecosystem services, including carbon sequestration, coastal protection, and biodiversity support. Accurate and automated delineation of mangrove extents from satellite imagery remains methodologically challenging due to spectral overlap with other dense vegetation types and the complexity of coastal environments.

The Automatic Mangrove Map and Index (AMMI) is a purpose-built spectral index that exploits the distinct reflectance behavior of mangrove canopies in the Near Infrared (NIR), Shortwave Infrared 1 (SWIR1), and Red bands. Unlike general-purpose indices such as NDVI or EVI, AMMI incorporates a two-component multiplicative structure that simultaneously suppresses open water and non-mangrove terrestrial signals while amplifying the spectral contrast characteristic of mangrove canopies.

Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument (MSI) imagery is well-suited for AMMI computation due to its 10–20 m spatial resolution across the relevant spectral bands and its high revisit frequency (~5 days), enabling temporally dense compositing for cloud-free analysis.

The AMMI index is computed from surface reflectance values (\rho) of three spectral bands:

Symbol

Band

Sentinel-2 Band

Wavelength

\rho_{NIR}

Near Infrared

B8A

~865 nm

\rho_{SWIR1}

Shortwave Infrared 1

B11

~1610 nm

\rho_{Red}

Red

B4

~665 nm

\text{Land} = \frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{Red}}{\rho_{Red} + \rho_{SWIR1}}

This ratio amplifies terrestrial vegetation signals while suppressing spectral contributions from open water and coastal sediment.

\text{Mangrove} = \frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{SWIR1}}{\rho_{SWIR1} - 0.65 \times \rho_{Red}}

The denominator scaling factor (0.65) is empirically calibrated to separate mangrove reflectance from other coastal woody vegetation.
AMMI = \frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{Red}}{\rho_{Red} + \rho_{SWIR1}} \times \frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{SWIR1}}{\rho_{SWIR1} - 0.65 \times \rho_{Red}}

Output Product

Description

Mangrove Binary Map

AMMI > 6

Presence/absence classification

Mangrove Density Index

AMMI > 5

Continuous canopy density visualization

Note: These thresholds were established by Suyarso & Avianto (2022) based on field validation in Indonesian mangrove ecosystems. Site-specific recalibration may be warranted when applying AMMI in geographically distinct regions.

from matplotlib.patches import Patch

from cartopy.mpl.gridliner import LONGITUDE_FORMATTER, LATITUDE_FORMATTER

cartoee.GeoAxes = cartoee.GeoAxesSubplot = GeoAxes
cartoee.ccrs = ccrs

cartoee.LATITUDE_FORMATTER = LATITUDE_FORMATTER

s2_base = (ee.ImageCollection('COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED')
    .filterBounds(batas_wilayah)
    .filterDate('2024-01-01', '2025-12-01')
    .filter(ee.Filter.lt('CLOUDY_PIXEL_PERCENTAGE', 20))
)

s2 = (s2_base
    .linkCollection(csPlus, ['cs_cdf'])
    .map(maskS2CSPlus)
    .map(scale_image)
    .median()
    .clip(batas_wilayah)
)

RED   = s2.select('B4')
NIR   = s2.select('B8A')
SWIR1 = s2.select('B11')

AMMI = s2.expression(
    '((NIR - RED) / (RED + SWIR1)) * ((NIR - SWIR1) / (SWIR1 - (0.65 * RED)))',
    {'NIR': NIR, 'RED': RED, 'SWIR1': SWIR1}
).rename('AMMI')

# Binary map (presence/absence)
AMMI_ts = AMMI.gt(6).selfMask().rename('AMMI_binary')

# Density map (continuous)
AMMI_density = AMMI.updateMask(AMMI.gt(5)).rename('AMMI_density')

colors_ammi = ['#0000FF', '#00FFFF', '#FFFF00', '#008000']
ammiVis = {'min': 5, 'max': 25, 'palette': colors_ammi}
fcVis   = {'bands': ['B8A', 'B11', 'B4'], 'min': 0, 'max': 0.3}
binVis  = {'palette': ['#008000']}

Gridlines are rendered at 0.1° intervals in WGS84 / PlateCarree projection. Colorbars are attached to panels (b) and (c); a categorical legend (Mangrove / Non-Mangrove) is placed on panel (d).

Threshold generalizability: The AMMI thresholds (> 5 and > 6) were optimized for Indonesian mangrove ecosystems. Application to other biogeographic regions may require field-validated recalibration.

Band selection: This implementation uses B8A (red edge NIR, ~865 nm) rather than B8 (~842 nm) for the NIR component. B8A has a narrower bandwidth and is generally preferred for vegetation index computation due to reduced atmospheric noise, though users should verify consistency with the original AMMI formulation.

Temporal compositing: A two-year median composite (2024–2025) minimizes cloud contamination but may smooth phenological variation. Seasonal analyses are recommended for monitoring studies.

No area calculation: This notebook focuses on visualization. For areal extent quantification, apply ee.Image.reduceRegion() with pixel area weighting (ee.Image.pixelArea()).

A QGIS Processing toolbox script that calculates any normalized difference spectral index from one or two raster layers using the universal formula:\text{NDI} = \frac{\text{Band A} - \text{Band B}}{\text{Band A} + \text{Band B}}

EE CHIRPS RainMapper is a lightweight, browser-based WebGIS tool built entirely inside the Google Earth Engine (GEE) Code Editor. It lets users draw or upload an Area of Interest (AOI) and instantly analyze rainfall accumulation and trends using the CHIRPS

Repositori di GitHub

A no-code Google Earth Engine App for exploring, analyzing, and downloading CHIRPS precipitation data through an interactive WebGIS interface.

Live App: 

https://​defaniarman​.users​.earthengine​.app​/view​/ee​-chirps​-rainmapper

Author: Defani Arman Alfitriansyah
Affiliation: Faculty of Forestry and Environment, Universitas Kuningan

EE CHIRPS RainMapper is a Google Earth Engine (GEE) App built entirely with the ui module, designed to remove the friction of manually processing CHIRPS rainfall data (clipping to a region, summing over time, computing annual averages, and generating trend charts). All processing is handled server-side on GEE and delivered through a browser interface, without requiring the user to write or modify any code.

The app supports drawing a custom Area of Interest (AOI), selecting between CHIRPS Daily or Pentad datasets, running one of three analysis modes, and exporting results as GeoTIFF or chart-derived CSV. The interface is fully bilingual (English/Indonesian) and includes an automatically generated narrative summary comparing the selected period against a historical baseline.

Custom AOI drawing — polygon or rectangle, drawn directly on the map, with a clear/reset option

Dataset selection — CHIRPS Daily (~5 km, 1981–present) or CHIRPS Pentad (~5 km, 1981–present)

Three analysis modes:

Per Period — total precipitation over a user-defined date range

1-Year Average — annual total plus a monthly precipitation trend chart

Multi-Year — multi-year average plus an interannual trend chart with linear trendline

Dynamic min/max stretching computed per AOI, using the official CHIRPS visualization palette

Descriptive statistics — mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and AOI area, computed via ee.Reducer combinations

Automatic narrative summary — compares the selected period’s mean rainfall against a 1991–2020 historical baseline, generated in both English and Indonesian

Data export — GeoTIFF download via getDownloadURL(), and chart data exportable as CSV/SVG/PNG through the built-in Google Charts menu

Bilingual interface — toggle between English and Indonesian without reloading the page, driven by a single translation dictionary

Dark basemap with light UI panels — custom Google Maps JSON style applied only to the basemap layer

Rainfall accumulation computed with ImageCollection.sum() over the filtered date range, per mode

Min/max values for map stretching are computed per AOI via reduceRegion() with ee.Reducer.minMax() rather than using fixed values, so the color scale adapts to each region and period

Descriptive statistics computed with a combined reducer chain (mean, median, stdDev, min, max)

Historical baseline fixed at 1991–2020 (or capped at current year − 1 if that range is unavailable), following the WMO convention for 30-year climate normals

This plugin consolidates the recurring, otherwise manual steps of a field-based baseline GIS assessment into one QGIS sidebar panel, mapped to the stages a GIS consultant normally works through on this kind of survey:

Workflow stage

What a GIS consultant would otherwise do manually

Toolkit feature(s) covering it

1. Field data ingestion

Manually export KoboToolbox submissions, geocode them, rebuild geometry from geopoint/geotrace strings

Kobo Connect

2. Field evidence handling

Manually download attachment URLs one by one, resize/rotate images, link them back to the right feature

Foto di Layer, Foto Explorer

3. Data QA/QC

Write ad hoc QGIS expressions to find missing coordinates, duplicates or incomplete records

Quick Query

4. Base data preparation

Separately add web basemaps, WMTS/WMS/WFS services, local reference files, or set up the Earth Engine Python API and write scripts to pull imagery

Add Layer, Basemap Search (QMS), GEE Connect

5. Spatial analysis

Build a spatial index, reproject to a local UTM zone, and script a nearest-neighbor distance calculation by hand

Distance Analysis

6. Data delivery / integration

Export layers individually to the format each stakeholder needs, or manually run ogr2ogr/write SQL to push data into PostGIS

Export Data, Export to Database

7. Field logistics

Manually convert layers to GPX for GPS units

Export to GPX

8. Cartographic output

Manually compute grid cells and index labels for a multi-page map series/atlas

Grid Index

In short: it is not a single-purpose tool, but a packaged set of the repetitive KoboToolbox-to-QGIS-to-deliverable steps a GIS consultant would otherwise re-implement per project, built specifically for the Gayo coffee farmer baseline survey (Konsorsium Konservasi Kopi Gayo) in Aceh Tengah and Bener Meriah, Aceh. Every tool is exposed as a QWidget page inside a single QDockWidget (see 

System architecture for the full technical breakdown), and the Grid Index step is also registered as a standalone QgsProcessingAlgorithm so it can be scripted or batch-run from the Processing Toolbox instead of the panel.

Brings field survey data collected in KoboToolbox into QGIS, so the baseline survey can be mapped and analyzed spatially instead of staying as raw form data

Log in with the KoboToolbox API URL, username and password -> list the user’s forms -> pick a form and its geometry field -> the plugin authenticates and downloads every submission (paginated) -> flattens nested/repeat-group answers and parses the geometry -> builds a feature collection and loads it as a QGIS layer

A QGIS vector layer with one feature per submission, all survey answers as attributes

Foto di Layer (Kobo)

Lets field photos taken during the survey be seen directly on the map next to the point that was surveyed, instead of digging through a folder of image files

Pick the survey layer and its photo field(s) -> the plugin detects which fields hold photo attachments and which field is the ID/title -> choose a download folder -> it downloads each photo from Kobo (authenticated), resizes it and fixes its EXIF rotation, then saves it under a predictable filename -> adds a virtual “path” field pointing to the saved file -> builds a map tip and configures the attribute form to preview the photo

Gives a quick way to browse and quality-check all the photos attached to repeated question groups in a Kobo form (e.g. multiple tree photos per plot), without opening each submission one by one

Connect to the Kobo form -> the plugin detects image fields inside repeat groups -> fetches submissions and builds one browsable entry per photo -> pick a photo in the list to download it on demand and preview it full-size

Quick Query

Speeds up day-to-day data checking: finding a specific respondent, filtering by a field value, or spotting bad/incomplete records, without writing a QGIS expression by hand every time

Pick the layer -> use the search box (text/attribute search), the filter box (field + operator + value), or a ready-made QC preset (e.g. “empty geometry / no coordinates”) -> the plugin builds the matching QGIS expression and applies it as a layer filter or selection

5

Distance Analysis

Answers the baseline assessment’s core spatial question - how far is each surveyed coffee farm from a forest area, and what is that forest area’s legal/conservation status - which is needed to flag encroachment risk

Pick the survey point layer and the forest/kawasan polygon layer plus its status field -> the plugin builds a spatial index of the forest polygons and picks a local UTM zone for accurate metric distances -> for every point it finds the nearest forest polygon, the distance to it, and its status field value -> converts the distance to m/km -> either draws a line from each point to its nearest forest (for visual QC) or writes the distance/status straight into new columns on the point layer

New distance + forest-status columns on the point layer, and/or a line layer showing each point-to-forest connection, plus a summary of the results

Export to GPX

Turns survey points/lines into a track/waypoint file that can be loaded onto a handheld Garmin GPS for offline field navigation, where QGIS itself isn’t available

Pick the point or line layer and a field to use as each point’s name (or leave it blank to dissolve everything into one named track) -> the plugin runs it through QGIS’s native Processing algorithms to fix geometries, convert polygons to lines if needed, dissolve/split features and set the name field -> writes the result using GDAL’s GPX driver

Grid Index

Produces the index grid needed to print or export the survey area as a multi-page map series/atlas (a common requirement for field teams and reports), instead of working with one unmanageably large map

Set the area extent, map scale, page size and rotation -> the plugin’s Processing algorithm checks whether the layer’s CRS is projected or geographic (transforming to World Mercator EPSG:3395 first if geographic, so cell sizes stay accurate) -> computes grid cells covering the extent at the chosen scale/page size and labels each one

Independent project. This is a community plugin, made out of

uses no GBIF logo. The data belong to their publishers and come with no
guarantee of quality or completeness — see the


GBIF data user agreement.

Comma-, semicolon- or newline-separated lists for the first three.

Within a step, multiple values are OR-ed; different steps are AND-ed.

Choose under Add to map:

Points — fetches up to Max records (10–5,000, default 500) in pages of
300 and adds a GeoJSON point layer. When the area is Country or World,
the map zooms to the fetched records.

Density — adds a raster tile layer from GBIF’s ad-hoc map API
(classic.poly style, hexagon bins, 40 hexagons per tile, 85 % opacity)
that shows every matching record, not only the fetched ones. Nothing is
downloaded record by record, so it is instant even for millions of records.

Both — the density layer plus the point layer.

Points, counter and density tiles are built from the same filter parameters,
so they always describe the same set of records.

A map view wider than the world or crossing the antimeridian drops the
longitude range instead of sending an inverted one.

iNaturalist photos (the biggest photo source in GBIF) are shown in their

All panel and popup content is built through the DOM API, never
innerHTML, so nothing from an API response is parsed as markup.

GEEDEF is a cloud-based, interactive land cover classification tool built entirely within the Google Earth Engine (GEE) Code Editor using the GEE JavaScript API. It is designed to accelerate supervised land cover mapping workflows at regional and local scales using Sentinel-2A Surface Reflectance (SR) Harmonized imagery.

The tool integrates three scientifically established machine learning classifiers — Random Forest (RF), Gradient Tree Boost (GTB), and Support Vector Machine (SVM) — operating over a 26-variable feature space composed of 10 native spectral bands and 16 derived spectral indices. The entire workflow, from image compositing and sample digitization to accuracy assessment and GeoTIFF export, is executed server-side on Google’s distributed computing infrastructure.

Test with a small ROI first before processing large areas to avoid computation time-outs.

Use Cloud Score+ as the primary masking method for tropical regions like Indonesia, where thin cirrus and coastal aerosols are common.

For mangrove studies, use Median Dry Season composite to maximize spectral contrast between mangrove canopy and aquaculture ponds (tambak).

Distribute samples spatially across the study area. Avoid concentrating all samples in one geographic location.

For SVM with RBF kernel, perform a manual grid search over C and gamma before the final classification run.

Check sample placement; avoid transitional zones; add more samples; merge spectrally similar classes

Class missing from output

Coordinates from iNaturalist’s geojson field are already WGS84
lon/lat, so no reprojection is needed (unlike the QGIS version of this
extractor, which has to transform into the project CRS).

“Active layer extent” reads whichever layer is currently selected in the
Layers panel via getSelectedLayerId(); if nothing is selected, pick a
layer from the dropdown that appears once “Active layer extent” is chosen.

The iNaturalist iconic_taxa=Animalia filter is narrower than it looks:
the API (and website) treat “Animalia” as animals not covered by any
other iconic taxon (so mostly invertebrates other than molluscs, insects
and arachnids), not literally every animal. This is iNaturalist’s own
behaviour, not something this plugin can change.

Place ID and Project are still limited by the Area (the API ANDs every
filter), so a place outside the current map view returns nothing. Tick
Ignore the Area in the advanced section to search the whole place or
project; it requires at least one other filter so it can’t pull the latest
observations from the entire world.

A photo license filter only matches observations that have a photo under
that license, so photo-less observations are excluded when it is set.

Annotations, taxon IDs and place IDs are exact IDs from iNaturalist (see its
“How to use iNaturalist Search URLs” help page); the annotation dropdowns
cover the six most common controlled terms.

The browser can’t set a custom User-Agent header the way the QGIS
plugin does, so requests go out with whatever the browser sends. Paging
still respects the “small/medium batch” limit in the UI, and requests are
spaced ~250 ms apart.

The plugin declares engines: ["maplibre"] only — it uses app.getMap()
directly for click/hover handling, which returns null on the Cesium
globe or the Mapbox renderer.

Everything this plugin builds on, in one place. “Reviewed” gives the version
or date of the material that was actually read while developing it.

Changelog

Area

What you get

Workspace (new in 1.11)

A ribbon like Microsoft Word: the Insert tab holds every element as large buttons; the Format tab shows the selection’s settings in two-row groups with captions — no side panel needed, no scrollbar. Contextual tabs Table Design / Table Layout for tables and Map Frame / Grid for map frames. Layers open as a drop-down over the canvas (drag to reorder); the full property panel and Ask AI stay closed until opened, so the page gets the whole width. Page orientation, border, grid, guides, snap and the selection-frame look (color, solid / dashed / dotted, width) sit in the status bar. Canva / Figma-style drawing with a live size badge, proportional corner resize (text scales its lettering), and a Hand tool that moves the content of map frames. On the desktop app, Save and Export open a Save as dialog to pick the folder.

Text like Word

Font, size, grow / shrink, change case, clear formatting, bold, italic, six underline styles, strikethrough, sub / superscript, effects, highlight and font colors; bullets and numbering (1. · 1) · (1) · a. · a) · A. · i. · I. · 1.1) with a hanging indent, indent, sort, alignment incl. justify, line / paragraph spacing, shading, borders and a quick Styles gallery. Text boxes hug their text. A Symbol dialog with 28 Unicode subsets (incl. a Map & GIS set), symbol fonts, character codes, recent symbols and special characters.

Charts (Plotly)

Bundled Plotly.js: donut, pie, column, bar, line, area, dots, lollipop, bubble, funnel, funnel area, treemap, sunburst, icicle, rose, radar, waterfall, histogram, box, violin and heat strip; Plotly, White, Minimal, Seaborn, ggplot2 and Dark styles; data from a layer (count, area, length, sum or average per class, in the layer’s class colors) or typed rows; exported as vector SVG.

Diagrams & HTML

Mermaid diagrams (flowchart, sequence, Gantt, pie, mind map, timeline, class, state…) with templates and themes, drawn as plain SVG. HTML blocks with your own HTML + CSS (sanitised, CSS scoped to the box), redrawn as SVG for export.

Tables like Word

Header / total row, first / last column, banded rows / columns, 8 table styles, border style, width, pen color and which borders, shading; a cell editor that inserts or deletes rows and columns at the chosen cell; AutoFit, distribute columns, 3 × 3 alignment, cell margins.

Map Series (atlas)

One layout, one page per feature of an index layer: the map frame zooms to each feature (or keeps its scale), text uses {series_name}, {series_page}, {series_count}, {series:FIELD}; page navigation in the ribbon and status bar; export the whole series as one multi-page PDF or one image per page.

Category Colors

Colour a GeoLibre layer by class from its own data: Distinct 200 (non-gradient), official KLHK class colours, Plotly, Tableau, ColorBrewer; opacity 100 % by default, outline, per-class edits; saved with the project and followed by the legends.

Map Tools

A Map Tools submenu of the Layout Composer menu (and a ribbon over the map) with the workflows of ArcGIS Pro Map Fundamentals: coordinates in DD · DMS · DDM · UTM · MGRS (typed or pasted in any format, conversion window, right-click copy with a custom template, cursor readout); go to coordinate, zoom to scale or layer; points, lines and polygons from coordinate lists, CSV / spreadsheet rows, WKT or GeoJSON — into a new or an existing layer; move or delete selected features; map chips as PNG + world file; image footprints and images covering a point.

Pictures

From a file or from a link; Remove background with 

remove.bg (your own API key); fit, fill, stretch, opacity, border, filters and masks.

Page

Size catalog grouped by type — ISO A0–A6, ISO B0–B5, Letter/Legal/Tabloid/ANSI/Arch, F4, Indonesian minimum sizes per map scale, posters, photo prints, presentation (16:9, 4:3, 16:10, 4K) and social media (Instagram post/portrait/story, TikTok/Reels, Facebook, X, LinkedIn, YouTube, Pinterest, WhatsApp). Units mm · cm · in · pt · px (px at a chosen pixels-per-inch), orientation, single/double neatline, margins, canvas grid, ruler guides, smart snapping.

Map frames

Live MapLibre map per frame, WYSIWYG at print scale, pan/zoom content (double-click), set or lock scale 1:n, rotation, zoom to layer, per-frame basemap (same as GeoLibre, streets, light, bright, satellite, topographic, none), GeoLibre capture mode that includes raster/COG layers.; frame shapes: rectangle, rounded, circle/ellipse, triangle, diamond, pentagon, hexagon, octagon, star, heart, shield, arch, or any image as a mask (PNG/SVG silhouette).; layers per frame: each frame shows its own set of GeoLibre layers (e.g. an inset with only the boundary), and linked legends follow.

Coordinate grids

DMS · DM · DD · UTM (m or km, auto zone), lines/crosses/dots, zebra or inside/outside ticks, labels inside/outside, BT/LS or E/W–N/S.

Inset / key maps

Extent box, location point or crosshair of another frame.

Legend

Built from GeoLibre symbology (match, step, interpolate), single-band rasters/COG as colormap ramps, XYZ / WMS tile layers with a thumbnail of the actual tile, editable labels/colors/order, manual entries, multi-column, LaTeX labels.

Attribute tables

Built from a layer’s features: summary by class (area in ha or km², length in km, count, sum or average of a field, with count and percent columns and a total row) or a feature list with chosen columns; filter (=, ≠, >, <, contains), sort, top N with “Other”, decimals and number format (1,234.56 or 1.234,56). Area and length are measured on the ellipsoid. Values update when the data changes.

Charts

Pie, donut (total in the centre), column and bar charts with the same data options; colors from the layer’s GeoLibre symbology, a palette or one color; labels as percent, value or class; legend beside the chart; axis ticks that never overlap.

Color bar

matplotlib-style: 39 colormaps + custom colors, reverse, continuous or classed, horizontal/vertical, pointed or square extensions (min/max/both), even/rounded/custom ticks with tick count, decimals, prefix/suffix, LaTeX title, reads min/max/colormap from GeoLibre raster (rasterState.rescale) or graduated layers.; values from a raster: min/max and colormap (incl. _r reversed) read from the layer’s stretch or statistics, with round tick values.

Scale bars

11 styles incl. dual units — by default the KLHK / topographic layout: round paper centimetres on top, kilometres below at the same ticks, every 0 aligned on the left, equal segments (first segment split on request) — numeric 1:n.

North arrows

26 styles plus your own PNG / SVG (kept in a reusable library), follow map rotation, letter U/N with adjustable size.

Canva-style editing

One click adds any item at the centre of the view (no box to draw); double-click or Enter edits text right on the page; text presets (heading, subheading, body, caption, map label, callout); text effects (shadow, lift, hollow, outline, highlight, neon, echo) and underline/strike/overline; flip horizontal/vertical for every item; image filters (brightness, contrast, saturation, grayscale, sepia, hue, blur + presets Mono, Vivid, Warm, Faded, Dramatic) and masks (circle, hexagon, star, heart, blob).

Text & LaTeX

Text boxes with variables ({title}, {date}, {scale}…), $…$ math anywhere (text, legend, color bar title, markers), formula item with 104-symbol catalog, structure templates and recent formulas (MathJax 3, vector output). Quick text bar: font (incl. installed fonts), size, bold, italic, color, alignment, superscript/subscript.; fonts: a searchable font picker with every Google Font (about 2,000 families, filter by sans, serif, display, script, mono, previewed in their own face) plus the fonts installed on your computer. Google Fonts are embedded in PNG, JPG, PDF and SVG exports.; typography: weight 100 to 900 (the weights each Google font really has), size, color and opacity, italic, small caps, underline, strikethrough, case, line height, letter spacing, paragraph gap, padding, left / centre / right / justified alignment, vertical alignment, and auto size (fixed box, auto height, or auto width).

Drawing

Polyline, polygon, Bézier pen (click = corner, drag = curve), freehand (simplified + smoothed), arrow line; 33 shapes; fills: solid, gradient, hatch patterns (/ \ × − | + ·); 6 dash styles.

Symbols

Point markers with labels (12 symbols); icon catalog with Maki (215) and Temaki (557) icons grouped by type (water, terrain, vegetation, transport, public services, health, education, religion, tourism, sports, utilities, hazards…) and Google Material Symbols (3,912 icons in 17 categories: maps, travel, transit, home, business…) in outlined, rounded or sharp style, regular or filled. The catalog searches as you type and loads icons in batches, and placed icons are stored in the layout so they work offline.

Effects

Drop shadow and frosted glass (blurs the map behind; reproduced in exports) on any item.

Editing

Minimal desktop-style workspace: every tool sits in the top bar (main menu and layout picker on the left; tools, map elements and insert menus in the centre; zoom, save and export on the right), outline icons that follow the light or dark theme, a full-height Layers panel, and an align, distribute and order bar at the top of the properties panel. Item properties grouped into Content, Style, Grid and Arrange tabs (or All); top-bar insert menus (Text, Draw, Shape, Image, Symbols, Scale bar), floating contextual toolbar for text and shapes, map navigation in the map panel (zoom in/out, fit layers, zoom to layer, previous/next extent), Move-content tool, collapsible left/right docks, item search, Figma-style selection (handles, rotation knob, size badge), hover outlines, multi-select, groups, align/distribute, lock/hide, rename, context menu, undo/redo, copy/paste, layers list. Round color wheel with brightness, hex, eyedropper, palette and recent colors. Light theme and soft neutral dark theme that follow GeoLibre.; precise position and size in mm, cm, in, pt or px, with a QGIS-style 9-point reference point, lock aspect ratio and ±90° rotation buttons.

Grid design

Canvas grid with spacing, major lines every N, lines or dots, color and opacity; layout grid like Figma (columns and rows with gutters and margin, shown on screen only, items snap to the edges); ruler guides plus guides at an exact position, guide color; adjustable snap distance and arrow-key nudge steps.

Layouts & templates

Several layouts per project, autosave, save/open .layout.json, save your own templates and start new layouts from them (maps re-framed on the current GeoLibre view).

QGIS templates

Export as .qpt: labels, map frames (extent, rotation, CRS EPSG:3857, DMS/DD/UTM grid with zebra frame), pictures, shapes, scale bars and legends become native QGIS items linked to their map; items QGIS has no equivalent for (color bars, charts, tables, north arrows, LaTeX, icons, drawings) are embedded as SVG pictures, so the page looks the same. Import .qpt from QGIS 3: page size, labels, maps (extents in EPSG:3857, EPSG:4326, WGS 84 / UTM and DGN95 / UTM), pictures, shapes, scale bars, legends, polylines and polygons. Checked by loading and rendering exported files in QGIS 3.44.

Export

PNG/JPG (75–600 dpi, page/white/transparent background), raster PDF, vector PDF, GeoPDF (every map frame georeferenced, WGS 84), SVG.; export settings open in their own window and a progress bar fills from left to right while maps render.

Download layout-composer-1.11.0.zip from 

Releases (or build it with python tools/build.py --release).

GeoLibre Desktop: copy the zip into %APPDATA%\org.geolibre.desktop\plugins (Windows) and restart GeoLibre — or install it from Manage Plugins in Settings once it is in the registry.

Enable Layout Composer in the Plugins menu. A Layout Composer menu with the plugin’s icon appears in GeoLibre’s menu bar: Open Layout Composer to design a print map, Back to the Map to return, plus Map Tools, the Map Tools ribbon and the tour.

Set the page in the status bar (Portrait / Landscape) or in the Page tab of the property panel (size catalog).

On the Insert tab click Map, then drag a box on the page (or click once for the default size). The Map Frame and Grid tabs appear: set the scale, basemap, frame and the coordinate grid there. Use the Hand to move what is inside the frame.

Add Legend, Color bar, North, Scale bar, Text, LaTeX, Table, Symbol, HTML, Mermaid, Data (tables and charts), Draw, Shape, Image, Symbols from the Insert tab. The Format tab shows the settings of whatever is selected; All properties (Arrange group) opens the full side panel.

Click the Export icon at the top right. A window opens with the format (PNG, JPG, PDF, Vector PDF, GeoPDF, SVG), resolution, background and file name; a bar shows the progress from left to right. To continue in QGIS, use Export as QGIS template (.qpt) in the main menu.

Mapping Mangrove Distribution Based on AMMI  (Suyarso & Avianto, 2022)

records.content:
Using Geemap (Wu, 2020) and Cartoee (Markert, 2019) Layout

Overview
This analysis demonstrates the application of the Automatic Mangrove Map and Index (AMMI) algorithm using Python-based geospatial tools to monitor mangrove ecosystems.

Tools and Libraries

ee (Earth Engine API)The core interface used to access Google Earth Engine’s cloud-based geospatial datasets and high-performance computing power.

geemap & geemap.cartoeeUsed to visualize GEE layers. cartoee specifically allows the creation of publication-quality static maps by integrating Earth Engine data with the matplotlib plotting environment.

matplotlib & cartopymatplotlib handles the overall figure layout, while cartopy provides tools for map projections, coordinate reference systems (CRS), and gridline generation.

AMMI Index (Automatic Mangrove Map and Index)

The Automatic Mangrove Map and Index (AMMI) is a specialized vegetation index designed to:

Identify mangrove extents automatically

Estimate canopy density

Unlike general vegetation indices, AMMI is optimized to distinguish mangroves from other coastal features.

Suyarso and P. Avianto (2022)Research Center for Oceanography, National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN, formerly LIPI), Indonesia.

Algorithm and Thresholding

The AMMI formula is derived from reflectance values (\rho) of:

NIR (Near Infrared)

SWIR1 (Shortwave Infrared 1)

Red band

1. Land Delineation\frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{Red}}{\rho_{Red} + \rho_{SWIR1}}

This component strengthens terrestrial signals while suppressing water and marine features.

2. Mangrove classification\frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{SWIR1}}{\rho_{SWIR1} - 0.65 \times \rho_{Red}}

This part is calibrated to capture mangrove extent and canopy density.

3. Complete AMMI FormulaAMMI =
\frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{Red}}{\rho_{Red} + \rho_{SWIR1}}
\times
\frac{\rho_{NIR} - \rho_{SWIR1}}{\rho_{SWIR1} - 0.65 \times \rho_{Red}}

Classification Thresholds

Mangrove Binary MapAMMI > 6

→ Classified as mangrove

Mangrove Density IndexAMMI > 5

→ Used to visualize canopy density variation

Prepared By
Defani Arman AlfitriansyahFaculty of Forestry, Universitas Kuningan

#!pip install geemap

from cartopy.mpl.gridliner import LONGITUDE_FORMATTER, LATITUDE_FORMATTER

cartoee.GeoAxes = cartoee.GeoAxesSubplot = GeoAxes
cartoee.ccrs = ccrs
cartoee.LONGITUDE_FORMATTER = LONGITUDE_FORMATTER
cartoee.LATITUDE_FORMATTER = LATITUDE_FORMATTER

# INITIALIZE EARTH ENGINE
ee.Authenticate()
ee.Initialize(project='ee-defaniarman')

# DEFINE REGION OF INTEREST FROM ASSET
batas_wilayah = ee.FeatureCollection(
    "projects/ee-defaniarman/assets/areakajian"
)

# LOAD CLOUD SCORE PLUS COLLECTION
csPlus = ee.ImageCollection(
    'GOOGLE/CLOUD_SCORE_PLUS/V1/S2_HARMONIZED'
)

# FUNCTION TO APPLY CLOUD SCORE PLUS MASK
def maskS2CSPlus(image):
    qa = image.select('cs_cdf')
    return image.updateMask(qa.gte(0.60))

# BASE SENTINEL-2 COLLECTION
s2_base = (ee.ImageCollection('COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED')
    .filterBounds(batas_wilayah)
    .filterDate('2024-01-01', '2025-12-01')
    .filter(ee.Filter.lt('CLOUDY_PIXEL_PERCENTAGE', 20))
)

# FUNCTION TO SCALE REFLECTANCE
def scale_image(img):
    return img.multiply(0.0001).copyProperties(
        img, ['system:time_start']
    )

# APPLY MASKING AND CREATE MEDIAN COMPOSITE
s2_masked = (s2_base
    .linkCollection(csPlus, ['cs_cdf'])
    .map(maskS2CSPlus)
    .map(scale_image)
)

s2 = s2_masked.median().clip(batas_wilayah)

# SELECT BANDS FOR AMMI CALCULATION
RED   = s2.select('B4')
NIR   = s2.select('B8A')
SWIR1 = s2.select('B11')

# CALCULATE AMMI INDEX
AMMI = s2.expression(
    '((NIR - RED) / (RED + SWIR1)) * '
    '((NIR - SWIR1) / (SWIR1 - (0.65 * RED)))',
    {
        'NIR': NIR,
        'RED': RED,
        'SWIR1': SWIR1
    }
).rename('AMMI')

# THRESHOLD FOR BINARY AND DENSITY MANGROVE
AMMI_ts = AMMI.gt(6).selfMask().rename('AMMI_binary')
AMMI_density = AMMI.updateMask(AMMI.gt(5)).rename('AMMI_density')

# VISUALIZATION PARAMETERS
colors_ammi = ['#0000FF', '#00FFFF', '#FFFF00', '#008000']
ammiVis = {'min': 5, 'max': 25, 'palette': colors_ammi}
fcVis = {'bands': ['B8A', 'B11', 'B4'], 'min': 0, 'max': 0.3}
binVis = {'palette': ['#008000']}

# PREPARE MANUAL MATPLOTLIB COLORBAR
cmap_ammi = mcolors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    'ammi_cmap', colors_ammi
)
norm_ammi = mcolors.Normalize(vmin=5, vmax=25)
mappable_ammi = cm.ScalarMappable(norm=norm_ammi, cmap=cmap_ammi)
mappable_ammi.set_array([])

# GET BOUNDING BOX FOR CARTOEE REGION
bbox = batas_wilayah.geometry().bounds().getInfo()['coordinates'][0]
region = [
    min(x[0] for x in bbox),
    min(y[1] for y in bbox),
    max(x[0] for x in bbox),
    max(y[1] for y in bbox)
]

# CREATE 2X2 FIGURE WITH UNIFORM PLOT SIZES
fig, axs = plt.subplots(
    2, 2, figsize=(15, 15),
    subplot_kw={'projection': ccrs.PlateCarree()},
    layout='constrained'
)

# ADD LETTER IN CIRCLE (TOP LEFT)
def add_letter(ax, letter):
    ax.annotate(
        letter, xy=(0.05, 0.95), xycoords='axes fraction',
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.3", fc="white", ec="black", lw=1),
        ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, zorder=100, weight='bold'
    )

# PLOT 1: FALSE COLOR
cartoee.add_layer(axs[0, 0], s2, region=region, vis_params=fcVis)
cartoee.add_gridlines(axs[0, 0], interval=0.1, linestyle=":")
axs[0, 0].set_title('False Color (B8A/B11/B4)', fontsize=14)
add_letter(axs[0, 0], 'a')

# PLOT 2: AMMI RAW
cartoee.add_layer(axs[0, 1], AMMI, region=region, vis_params=ammiVis)
cartoee.add_gridlines(axs[0, 1], interval=0.1, linestyle=":")
axs[0, 1].set_title('AMMI Raw', fontsize=14)
add_letter(axs[0, 1], 'b')
cbar1 = fig.colorbar(
    mappable_ammi, ax=axs[0, 1], orientation='vertical',
    shrink=0.8, pad=0.03
)
cbar1.set_label("AMMI Value")

# PLOT 3: AMMI DENSITY
cartoee.add_layer(
    axs[1, 0], AMMI_density, region=region, vis_params=ammiVis
)
cartoee.add_gridlines(axs[1, 0], interval=0.1, linestyle=":")
axs[1, 0].set_title('Mangrove Density (>5)', fontsize=14)
add_letter(axs[1, 0], 'c')
cbar2 = fig.colorbar(
    mappable_ammi, ax=axs[1, 0], orientation='vertical',
    shrink=0.8, pad=0.03
)
cbar2.set_label("AMMI Density Index")

# PLOT 4: AMMI BINARY
cartoee.add_layer(axs[1, 1], AMMI_ts, region=region, vis_params=binVis)
cartoee.add_gridlines(axs[1, 1], interval=0.1, linestyle=":")
axs[1, 1].set_title('Mangrove Binary (>6)', fontsize=14)
add_letter(axs[1, 1], 'd')

# ADD LEGEND TO THE TOP RIGHT BOX OF PLOT 4
legend_elements = [
